utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ossogo, you have some matters to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, just a small question. I already spoke to our colleagues from the Defence concerning Mr. Alarid. It's a motion which we filed on the 18th of August to admit certain documents and we still don't have a decision on this motion and in this motion there was a document to help both the Chamber and the Defence to the proposal to go and see the place. We had announced that during the -- this paper we call 360 degrees - waiting for the decision on this motion I would like to note if I can use some pictures of this programme. They have been taken at Bikavac and the witness will tell us exactly where it was. Therefore, I spoke to my colleagues of the Defence and they didn't oppose this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. I see no objection to your using it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't call the witness yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness VG-115.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did you sleep well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I slept well for a couple of hours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Very well. So I see you will be up to answering the last questions I have to ask you in this case. I'd like to come back on the events concerning the torching which took place in the Pionirska Street and for this, Mr. President, could we go into private session because of the information which shouldn't be made public?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: where you observed the flames, fire.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Then could you put an arrow, mark an arrow, on the Pionirska Street, a few centimetres, perhaps 5 centimetres, to show Pionirska Street. If you remember --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you indicate at what place you saw the smoke. Where was the smoke coming out from? If you don't remember, never mind.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could this be admitted for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is admitted as P31, Exhibit P31. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, perhaps it would be useful to know what was the house which was torched. Maybe you could ask the witness what was the house which was torched. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Witness VG-115, could you indicate, in case you know, which was the house which was torched and where you saw all the smoke coming from and the fire and the flames which you saw.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the screen or on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: On the photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Mr. President, we shall continue our questions about the incident in Pionirska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Witness VG-115, the next day after the fire took place in the Pionirska Street, did Milan Lukic visit you, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: What was his appearance? How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan wore a camouflage uniform; he was armed, as always; and he had a bandaged hand, one of his hands had a bandage.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Do you remember which hand had this bandage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember. Certainly it was only one hand. I'm sorry, but I can't remember which.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Right. Did he explain to anybody why he was wearing this bandage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, normally people asked him, What's that with your hand? And Milan answered, I injured my hand last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: When you say "people," do you remember who he spoke to in the company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody there knew Milan, both the men and the women. I knew him personally also but I never asked him about his hand, so I could not tell the Court what had happened to his hand but he said himself that he had injured it on the previous night.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness VG-115, we shall now speak of another incident, an incident which happened before that. In 1992, I would like to ask you if you remember that Milan's group (redacted) and pushed out Muslims, asked Muslims to quit --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would object that this is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You cannot lead on matters of this kind. It is leading. Reformulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did it happen in 1992 that Milan Lukic (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll allow that. He can ask whether Milan Lukic

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What he did, just ask what he did when he came there. Give the answer first. Witness, did Milan Lukic (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milan Lukic (redacted) often, but one day, as the gentleman mentioned in his question, they were making plans. (redacted) I saw a convoy of cars and people (redacted) and they wanted to take away (redacted) There were women and men alike. (redacted) (redacted) and I was able to warn many people to hide anywhere, that something bad was going on, and I felt that they would be taken away (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) But Milan Lukic was able to find three (redacted) and take them away. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You must take over from here, Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: When Mr. Milan Lukic arrived with his group, did he speak to you or did one of the members of his group speak to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long time ago and I don't remember well, but somebody (redacted) and shouted and asked questions about where the other people were. It's -- they seemed to suspect me, but it was my duty to protect those people. They were not armed and they -- without any protection. They were simply doing their jobs. They were not active in politics. And they needed shelter, they needed to be saved, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they were taken to the cars and driven away, soon after that we heard shots and I suspected that they were killed on the new bridge over the Drina, the newly built bridge. It was at day-time, unfortunately, they never even respected the curfew. They didn't care whether it was night or day, whether people would see or hear them or not. They would go about their business at any time. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) I soon understood that in the town of Visegrad among the Muslim population much injustice had been done to them. They were people who did not take part in the war. They were civilians, unprotected people, elderly people, women, girls, children. The Lukics did not fight for their territory, the Serbian republic. They were making massacres, killing innocent population. In June, July, August, after that there was no single Muslim left in Visegrad, no children, no elderly people. I'm sorry, I'm sitting here without being able to prove that with photographs. There were shootings, executions, every day on the Drina after 3.00 in the afternoon. Over a hundred men from the Varda company from town, from the surrounding villages, on a daily basis. The Drina was all foamy with blood --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I have to stop you there. Thank you very much, Witness VG-115. I have to stop you there. We will continue the examination on one specific aspect which you observed concerning the activities of Milan Lukic and his cousin, that was the torching at Bikavac. Was there a fire in the area of Bikavac to your knowledge and what year was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That also happened in late June 1992, after the incident in Pionirska Street, after the great massacre in the house of Adem Omeragic and there was a huge massacre in Bikavac in the house of Meho Aljic, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you describe what you observed in this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It was in the afternoon. I was -- I cared much about my family house in which I was left alone. And I cared a lot about the old married couple, the Subasics (redacted) Pasan and Aisa Subasic. Their houses were (redacted) nearby in Bikavac. (redacted) Those two -- that elderly couple were left alone. They were over 80 years of age and I went to see them often to be -- to bring them some food because you couldn't buy anything. All the shops were closed, you couldn't go to any shop and buy anything. And on that day I went to my house which had been newly furbished to -- for living in. (redacted) (redacted) I went to my house to fetch some coffee, sugar and washing powder to take them to that elderly couple to help them. Before that, I met them and they told me how they were hiding because they were living in a newly built building. There was also a wartime shelter there, and they were saying, We've been hiding for days in your house with many neighbours from the neighbourhood. Upon returning from my house I saw a convoy of vehicles. They couldn't reach the houses because the road was, or rather, the street was very narrow, not wide enough for cars to pass. I recognised Milan Lukic's car and the cars of other members of his groups. They had taken those cars from Muslims. There were many cars and many people, and there were many people from Gostilja who I recognised and they were all being taken to the house of Meho Aljic, (redacted) (redacted) And then I went to a small orchard, on the right-hand side there were plum trees, small plum trees.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ossogo, Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have different approaches to how witnesses are to be led. I don't particularly favour the narrative approach, where a witness goes on and on and on and on. I'd much rather the approach where counsel asks the witness a question, the witness answers shortly, and then another question is asked. I also believe that in this case that approach would have an additional advantage in relation to a witness who is obviously distraught.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. In fact, I wanted to interrupt the witness, but there can be a consequence which is that the logic of the ideas -- the witness is indeed traumatised, as you may have noticed more than once, and several times since she arrived here we have been in private session and outside this chamber we noticed that the witness was distressed and maybe this could have consequences on her health and have a problem about what she wants to say. But I agree with you that this approach -- another approach would be better to have the proper answers. Now the narrative is finished, I could ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness VG-115, for what you've just said. Could we come back on one aspect what you observed before we go on. Could you indicate to us where you were when the group of Milan Lukic went to the house of Mr. Meho, did you say, Meho Aljic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: (redacted) from where did you see the arrival of the -- the entry of the group of Milan Lukic as you indicated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were standing on this very narrow road in front of me. If you have photographs, I can show you that road. They were standing in front of me. There was no way I could bypass them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You spoke about a photograph. We are going to come to that. Did you recognise the members of that group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could recognise the members of the group because I had come to know them very well (redacted) Among them there were also citizens of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you give their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall do my best to remember them all. Milan Lukic was there, Sredoje Lukic, so Milan Lukic with his father, Mile; with his brother Gojko Lukic; then Niko Vujicic was there, a policeman in the town of Visegrad; Veljko Planincic, a police officer in the town of Visegrad who was called Razinoda; then Radoje Simsic (redacted) an elderly man was also there; Oliver Krsmanovic who was a haulier from Visegrad was also there; Caruga from Pljevlja was there, I don't know his first and last names; then Slobodan Roncevic was there (redacted) (redacted) he was a student from Novi Sad who hailed from Montenegro. Then there was Mitar whom -- Mitar Vasiljevic, Mitar -- the senior Mitar; then there was Knezevic who didn't have an eye; there was Zoran from the vicinity of Belgrade from Ostruznica; then there was -- whether he was Vasiljevic or Simsic I don't know for sure but I know him well and I can recognise him well. There are other members of Lukic's group whose names I cannot remember but whom I could recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: What did they do after that? You saw them and what did they do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the right side. There was a small fence which I could go over to go into a plum orchard. This path I could take in order to avoid the road. They were taking the people to Meho Aljic's house. There were people from the village of Gostilja whom I recognised there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) I don't know what his name was, an elderly man. They were pulling the door of the garage of Meho Aljic's house and they actually blocked the house door with the garage door, they placed it under the window of the living-room which was facing the road. I could make out very well (redacted) who entered the house of Meho Aljic among the last people to enter. Milan was shouting and yelling at them and these were the last people I remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you, Witness VG-115. I would like to ask you, at that stage did you see people who were obliged, forced, to go into this house of Meho Aljic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you identify them for the Bench, as far as you can remember.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recall well. Do I have to say all the names of this family, of the members of this family right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: If you could, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: It was the Turjacanin family, Djulka Turjacanin; her daughter Zehra Turjacanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you again. I gave you a sheet of paper yesterday and the second sheet of paper had a pseudonym. The first name you mentioned is VG-114.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You may continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it is the Turjacanin family. Djulka Turjacanin; VG-114, Zehra Turjacanin, I'm not quite sure what her married last name is; and a small daughter of Djulka Turjacanin (redacted) and she was mentally challenged, she couldn't think properly and she couldn't speak properly, she was 10 at that time. I have forgotten the child's name. And Zehra Turjacanin also had a small child who was there and this was the last family to enter the house of Meho Aljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Yes, we'll pause here, VG-114 is Zehra Turjacanin and not Djulka. Could the transcript please be corrected? You may continue and give the names of the people which you saw forced to go into the house of Meho Aljic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not quite understand the question. I was focusing on VG-114 and therefore I didn't quite get to your question. Would you please be so kind as to ask me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Yes, certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise, just one technical issue, do we have redaction of the name here because it would be in public, this VG-114 is --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are still in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Okay, because it is protected witness and we have a full name now in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Yes, Witness VG-115. I will repeat my question. Could you please continue and give us the names of the families you knew and who were forced to go into the house of Meho Aljic. You mentioned the chief of the family, you mentioned VG-114. So please could you continue and give us the names of the people you recognised and who were forced into that house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've stated -- no, these were mostly people from Gostilja. I have stated the names of the Murtic's family. These people lived in the surrounding villages and I couldn't remember their names. I didn't know their names, but I did know the Turjacanin family very well (redacted) (redacted) So of the Turjacanins there were four female members of that family and a child, Dzehva Turjacanin's child.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. So all these people were forced to enter into Meho's house by the Lukic's group, and then what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that while they were pulling this garage door, I suppose that they would be setting the house on fire and that indeed happened. So I took this cross path via this plum orchard to come to the main road. I was descending down towards the town. I had no more time to drop in on the two elderly people, the elderly couple with the little bag that I was carrying. The protected witness and these other Turjacanin persons whom I mentioned they all saw me personally as I was entering the orchard which belonged -- the land belonged to Medo Mulahasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Mulahasic or members of his family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Around this house or next to his house were there other relatives of his that were living there, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Medo lived in Medo Mulahasic's house, as well as his wife Sevala, as well as their two daughters, the name of one was Hanka and I forgot the name of the other daughter. These girls were married and he also had two sons who lived in Serbia. So Medo and Sevala Mulahasic lived alone because their children had scattered every which way and the elderly married couple lived alone. But on that day I did not see Sevala or Medo Mulahasic. Later, I saw an incident in town involving Medo Mulahasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: VG-114 [as interpreted], among the people who were forced to enter Meho Aljic's house was a person that you said that was in that group. So do you know whether he lived close to Meho's house or can you tell us where he lived exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very near.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I will now give you a map which you asked for, and that way you'll be able to show us on the map where is Meho Aljic's house, where this event occurred, this dramatic event occurred. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Witness VG-115, I would now like to ask you the following. After these people were forced to enter into Meho's house, Meho Aljic's house, from where you stood and where you were observing things, what exactly did you hear or see afterwards? You told us about shots; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could see how they were throwing bottles filled with petrol and set afire and I could see them firing bursts of fire toward the window, and they were throwing, very energetically, hand-grenades. And then I had to go away, I had no time to call on the elderly couple. I went toward the town centre. I was walking down the street in Bikavac. There was much noise, there were explosions, and they were doing the same thing as in Pionirska, but at Bikavac I was able to see it with my own eyes. And I stand behind my statement, I back it up fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. When you started describing that incident you gave us the name of people who were forced to enter this house. I would like to ask you whether after this event you ever met these people again. Do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since that event, I haven't met anyone of the Turjacanin family. I met a man from the Murtic family. He came to see me and told me more about that incident. I had seen his wife and his mother and his uncle. What the -- I never met anyone from the Turjacanin family again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You say that you met a relative of the Murtic family, a man, who told you about the incident. What did he say exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said to me that in the house that belonged to Meho Aljic his mother, his wife, and his uncle had burned and that he had escaped from the village of Gostilja, that they didn't find him at his home. He also told me what he had heard, that there was a surviving witness, a woman from the Turjacanin family. I'm very glad that she survived that tragedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that you are glad she survived, who are you talking about exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I free to mention her name now so I don't create a mess? Can I mention the name of this survivor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We are in private session? Yes, yes, it may be mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The survivor is Zehra Turjacanin, she was a girl of about 23 then. I know her very well. She had long hair and was a pretty girl. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Witness VG-115, I have a few questions to ask before we are done with this Bikavac incident. Earlier you said that Milan Lukic was yelling, yelling at these people that he had forced into Meho Aljic's house. He was yelling, but were you able to make anything of what he was saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was shouting at them to make them enter the house faster because people resisted, especially the Turjacanin family.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You're saying that he was shouting, was he just screaming or was he uttering words; and if he was uttering any words, do you remember what these words were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Milan Lukic never said anything to me. He was shouting at the people who he wanted to make enter Meho Aljic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you say that he threw flammable products into the house as well as hand-grenades. What were these flammable products, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to the extent that I could see, they had something like bottles filled with gasoline or some flammable material; and the hand-grenades were like, you know, those small hand-grenades that made a lot of noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: But were you able to identify who was doing this amongst that group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the members of his group, although Milan was most prominent. I had very little time. I didn't dare stay on longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I understand you well, but you are saying that Milan was leading the group. I'm sorry that I ask. Could you tell us exactly what he did. You said that he was -- he opened the garage, he was yelling at these people who were forced into that house and who lost their lives in the house later on, but were you able to see anything else that he did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan was dragging the metal garage door which was put against the main door of the house. The garage was actually part of the house. They leaned that garage door against the door of the house to prevent the people from coming out. I could see all that from my vantage point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. So he did this to prevent the people from getting out of the house, and it was after that that the hand-grenades were thrown. Was he one of the people throwing the hand-grenades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was several of them, but Milan was in charge. He stood out and it was his voice that could be heard most, and I wasn't glad -- it wasn't at all pleasant for me to stand there and witness all that. I knew what was happening and I couldn't help anyone, it wasn't in my power.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Regarding Sredoje Lukic, could you give us some details as to what he did exactly during this incident. What exactly did he do? You told us what Milan Lukic was doing, but could you tell us what Sredoje was doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sredoje Lukic also shouted at the people, pushed them around, and helped Milan to drag the metal garage door to the entrance door. And he was also intimidating the people, so he was -- he wore a Balaclava not to be recognised, because he was a police officer in the town of Visegrad so everybody knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You already said that you knew him personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Sredoje Lukic personally. He in time of -- in times of peace he was a very kind person.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Then when the war started he changed; is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the war began, Sredoje changed a lot. He was a married man, a family man, with three children, his wife was Vicenka [phoen]. As far as I know, no family member of his was killed. He had no reason to behave that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. All these people you mentioned who were locked up in Meho Aljic's house, were they all civilians? You said that you knew them. Were they locals from the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people were all civilians. Nobody was armed or wore any kind of uniform. They were all regular citizens, civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I would now like to talk about an incident, another incident, the one that has to do with Mr. Gojko Lukic. You said that it is Lukic's brother, you identify him as such and you identify him as being -- as living with Lukic in the Pionirska house also with his parents. Was this person married?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the words of Gojko Lukic himself, he was married, his wife lived in Belgrade, and they had two sons. I don't know whether that is true and I don't feel like probing into that. He was Milan Lukic's elder brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Was his wife killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gojko Lukic met a young girl during the war, he met her at Visegrad; during the first months she was not his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: And what happened to this woman?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: (redacted) He needed fuel, and he said to me, Turn around and look out the window, that's my girlfriend Amela Gacka from Dobrun, the village of Dobrun.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Did you ever see this woman sitting in a car driven by Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed that woman in the Passat vehicle, but that was in late autumn, not on that day but in late autumn, a couple of months thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: After you met her, did you learn what happened to her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also had occasion to see her walking with Milan Lukic's mother. They would be carrying some groceries that they had bought at the green market, and I could notice that Amela Gacka was pregnant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Is she alive today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amela Gacka is no longer alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you tell us in which conditions she died, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was returning from the centre of town, from the public accountancy service (redacted) Amela Gacka was sitting by Milan in a car. He took her out and to the bridge, to the bridge over the Drina River. I remember, it had to be sometime around or before, rather, 1.00 p.m., during the day that is. She was the last victim that I know of in the city of Visegrad and this happened in autumn, in late autumn, it was cold. Actually, from what I learned Milan had her returned, had her specifically returned from Belgrade in order to cut short her young life. Amela Gacka had a father and a brother, Meho Gacka was the father and I forgot the name of the brother (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You say that he made her come back so that he would end her life. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean is that Gojko Lukic, his older brother, actually gave all that up and he was no longer noticed -- his presence was no longer noticed in these last months in Visegrad. He left the town together with Amela Gacka to build a future somewhere else with her and live with her somewhere else and she was also pregnant. Before giving birth and giving -- bringing a new life into this world, he brought her back to the Bosnian city of Visegrad and took her life. Otherwise Amela Gacka would also be a witness here today and she would have many a thing to tell about what Milan Lukic did. I'm very sorry for her and for her parents -- parent and her brother, whom I knew well, although I do not know where they are today nor whether they are still alive. I have no information whatsoever about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: When you say he cut short her life, who are you speaking about, Gojko or Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about Milan Lukic. In the last two months, Gojko was not anywhere to be seen in the city of Visegrad. He himself was saying that he would give it up, the city, go away, that he would go away to live with Amela Gacka. And he told me, I'm afraid that he might kill her, Amela, that is, one day because he also had killed her mother. I'm relating to you all these things which were told me by Gojko Lukic. I gave some thought to this man. He did so many things wrong, committed so many wrongdoings, but I do give -- I do have an inkling of hope for him because I'm very sorry about all the injustice that he has suffered. I am sorry that he has lost his wife and his unborn baby.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness VG-115.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have finished with my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ossogo. Mr. Alarid -- no, Mr. Alarid, you have of course every right to put your case vigorously, that's the tradition from which you come, but I ask you to bear in mind that this is a witness who has obviously been through quite a lot and is distraught. Take that into consideration and I know you'll be able to find a way to put your case as vigorously as possible, but nonetheless respecting her condition. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Ms. 115, good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'd kind of like to address the last things you just testified to, but I would like to get some background information as to how your involvement in the prosecution of Mitar Vasiljevic, Milan Lukic, and Sredoje Lukic occurred. Can we do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you frankly, I decided to do that myself, to testify, that is, and I did testify in order to prove in the minutest details that I know what the truth was as to what the Lukics did and what Mitar Vasiljevic did. Nobody compelled me to do this. I'm doing this on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, but that's actually exactly what I'd like to talk about. When did you make this decision to participate as a witness against Mitar Vasiljevic, Milan Lukic, and Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always had this decision in my subconscious. I couldn't have done it in the city of Visegrad because there I wasn't a free person. (redacted) (redacted) I knew that one day I would either be taking the witness-stand or writing a book about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Why would you want to write a book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would want to do that because the most beautiful of cities, Visegrad, which I love the most in the entire Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the currently Republika Srpska (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and now -- yes, please go ahead, ask your question. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Ma'am, isn't it true that you place personal responsibility for the destruction of Visegrad on my client, Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, and Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have to tell you this, Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, and all the other members of Milan's group always hoisted their huge black flag with a skull and bones on it on which was written "The Avenger." (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I haven't said you were lying yet.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not come here to lie. I have come here to prove the truth and that truth is a small thing, namely, what was it that those people did in the city of Visegrad. I'm not actually defending the Muslim people or the Serbian people for that matter; I'm just here to tell what I've seen and what I've experienced in order for all people to be done justice.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say to you even today, I do not feel the need to hate anyone, I cannot hate anyone, I was just ashamed and I'm still ashamed today. I never hated the Lukic family, not before the war, not during the war, nor do I hate them now. (redacted) (redacted) I fear them then, it was not that they feared me. Let me reiterate, I do not personally hate them, I do not hate any Serbs. I'm not protecting Muslims. I'm just telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true, ma'am, that despite the fact that you're supposedly in close proximity to several crimes, no one that participated in these crimes harmed you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evil was inflicted on me in other situations which are not of relevance in this particular case. Evil was inflicted on me for two and a half years in terms of the fact that I could not leave that city. Had I left it, it would have better for Lukic, (redacted) (redacted) Visegrad is a small town, everything is known, everything is heard as to what other people are doing. To their misfortune, I was there to see what they were doing and I should like to emphasize once again, I personally do not hate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Ma'am, ma'am, that's not the question I asked you. The question I asked you is: Supposedly you're in close proximity to the perpetrators of very serious crimes, they see you, they know you see them, they do not harm you; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. At that moment they inflicted no harm on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Don't you feel that that is illogical that you would not be harmed, especially since they supposedly hate you (redacted) (redacted) that you wouldn't be made a victim with the rest of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you specifically driving at? What was your specific question? Should Milan Lukic have killed me in Pionirska Street or the Bikavac settlement and then you would be happy with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I would not be happy with that. What I would happy with is if you would explain why a material witness to such horrible crimes, (redacted) is not included as a victim to -- in hindsight -- sure, so you wouldn't be here today but simply because you just said that you were hated as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did hate me. They're actually sorry today that I survived. The Lukics did have the time to kill me. They knew that I could not leave town, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Ma'am, let's -- you gave a statement and you said that you went on your own accord to give a statement against the Lukics and Vasiljevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Before you made the decision to give your testimony in either statement or trial, had you read news accounts or the indictment against Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So you had not read any accounts as to the facts and circumstances of the fire before you gave your statements over three days in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave statements, my statements, when Mitar Vasiljevic was deprived of liberty, that is when I made my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So when you saw the fact -- and I'm assuming you saw or got that information from news reports and the community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can assume that. I do not oppose that. I'm here to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: On direct exam by the state you testified that when you saw that Mitar Vasiljevic had been arrested he was fatter than you had known him before when he was -- when you were a witness to his atrocities; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mitar Vasiljevic had put on some weight by the time I saw him in the court, I mean he had gained some weight in relation to the last time I saw him in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true you said, though, that you had seen photographs of him following his arrest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I saw Mitar in the flesh in the city of Visegrad and after so many years had elapsed I saw Mitar as an arrested person. A couple of years had passed, so I couldn't help noticing, and I did say so, that Mitar had put on some weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: A couple of years had passed. You're giving your statement today in 2008 for instances that happened in 1992. Before 2001 when you gave your testimony, when was the last time you had seen Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was able to see Mitar Vasiljevic as long as I myself was in Visegrad. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, would the court usher please put on the screen what has been uploaded as 1D00-0596 which is the English version of Ms. 115's 2000 statement and 1D00-0616 is the B/C/S version. Now, ma'am, while they're uploading those documents, isn't it true that you've read them before your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I did not understand your question. What is it that you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you read your statement you gave to the Tribunal in 2000 prior to your testimony today to refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I skimmed through it. I didn't read it in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I would ask the court usher to direct the -- to page 14 of both respective statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you see that, ma'am? I'd like you to read the paragraph discussing Gojko Lukic, third paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About Gojko Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you testified today under oath on direct examination that you actually witnessed the death at the Drina River of his brother's wife; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a -- wait a minute. Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Isn't it true you never mentioned in your statement that you actually witnessed the murder?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this is a -- my condensed statement, a condensation of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Ma'am, don't you think it's an important thing to get out in a statement that you're an actual eye-witness to a crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I passed by in a car that day. I was returning (redacted) and Milan took out this pregnant girl from his car. I was alone and they were alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The Drina bridge is in the centre of town, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two bridges, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And things had returned to normal by this point supposedly that you had seen Gojko's wife in the market with his mother? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. That happened two or three days before the murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And at this particular time you're saying today that at 1.00 p.m. you were actually right there, conveniently, at the time that Gojko's wife was taken by Milan Lukic to the bridge to be killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was returning (redacted) (redacted) via the Novi Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you're saying today that you actually witnessed that killing; true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did he do it with a gun or a knife?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shots could be heard. He did it with fire-arms, not a knife.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How come you didn't say that in 2000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember word for word what it was that I said in 2000. I tried to provide as many details as possible, and now when you're asking me these things I'm giving you answers to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You reviewed the statement before signing them; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you reviewed them and actually issued a proofing statement or proofing notes that you also agreed to; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in the proofing statement you never mentioned the fact that you were actually an eye-witness to the death of Milan's sister-in-law; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here in this statement you can see that I was in a vehicle, and I also indicated here that Milan and Amela were also in a vehicle. And I stated that that was on the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And nowhere did you say in that statement that you actually witnessed the killing of his pregnant wife until today, here in court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked me specifically about this murder at that time there was -- Mitar Vasiljevic was on trial. So I say now, if I was alone in the vehicle on the bridge and Milan was in a vehicle on the bridge, I was not armed, Milan was armed, and Milan took the lady out on the bridge and it was common knowledge what happened to men and women when they were taken to that bridge. Nobody else was shot at. Milan did not shoot at me. Amela Gacka was killed then, and when I got back (redacted) and on the morrow and for some time after that this story was told and repeatedly told that Amela Gacka had been killed on the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So are you saying now that really you just heard that she had been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Milan was shooting while we were passing by, he was shooting at Amela. It was the talk of the town. It was a new story. It happened in late autumn. At the moment I happened to be there. We had to cross the bridge. The bridge is long, so we couldn't turn back in our vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Don't you find that's an amazing coincidence that you had -- and by the way, this is November, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And don't you find it's an amazing coincidence that you in a wrong-place/wrong-time situation just happened to witness so many atrocities personally by Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, and Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all happened by chance. It's -- it is incredible but it happened by chance -- but they did that on a daily basis so that everybody could have been in the position to witness something of that. To my misfortune, I had to go, or rather, take a ride from the town centre (redacted) so I happened to see the events on the bridge and the things that happened to people. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) Don't take me wrong. I wouldn't have had the courage to follow the Lukics around or members of their group to learn what they were doing. Nobody was opposing them nor did they care. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the Lukics and the members of the group were committing massacres and I knew what they were doing. They were doing what -- they were going about their job (redacted) I couldn't oppose them, nobody could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could the court usher please turn the statements to page 12, please, on both B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Ma'am, I'd like to put to your attention and ask you review the second paragraph and third and fourth paragraphs of your statement in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: On page 12, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Please indicate when you've finished reading.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you realize, ma'am, in your statement of 2000 before the trial of Mitar Vasiljevic, you were given every opportunity to describe the Bikavac fire; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, but here --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that you mentioned Mitar Vasiljevic, as in the one that was on trial, as being present at the Bikavac fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned Mitar Vasiljevic because there were two persons by that name. The one I know is the younger Mitar Vasiljevic who worked as a waiter in Panos and the older Mitar Vasiljevic, that was my mistake, is, in fact, Mitar Knezevic, an older man who only had one eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So, in fact, you do claim that Mitar Vasiljevic, the younger one that worked as a waiter, was at the Bikavac fire and you maintain that today; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that this is about Mitar Knezevic, who died a natural death.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So you're saying that this is a mistake now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I always designated them as Mitar Vasiljevic senior and Mitar Vasiljevic junior, and this one is Mitar Knezevic who was older than Mitar Vasiljevic, the waiter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So Mitar Vasiljevic now wasn't at the fire, as you testified earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When did I testify earlier? The first time I've given testimony about the Bikavac fire is today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But I'm talking about in your statement, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am now telling you what this statement means. I cannot remember the exact names of every person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well -- but you'd indicated that you'd known Mitar Vasiljevic for 20 years, that he'd been a local (redacted) and he was a waiter, a well-known person.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a well-known person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in your statement you indicate with such certainty that you saw him at Pionirska Street fire, the Bikavac fire, and several incidents of atrocities in late June and July of 1992; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I saw him --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so do you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- at the fire. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: At Pionirska Street fire and Bikavac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Mitar Vasiljevic in Pionirska Street and I pointed him out. He was on a -- he was on horseback, on a white horse, but it was Mitar Knezevic. I cannot remember well about Mitar Vasiljevic, the younger man. And I remember well all I said about those -- these other people. It was always confusing to me because there were two persons by the same name Mitar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But nothing that make them look alike, correct, or how you knew them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they don't look alike at all. Mitar Knezevic in my mind always was Mitar Vasiljevic, but he was older than the real Mitar Vasiljevic. And I repeat, he only had one eye, I don't remember which eye, but they were together often.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that you state in your statement with such certainty that Mitar Vasiljevic was committing atrocities with -- supposedly with Milan in late July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President, I wonder whether one could continue, with all respect due to my colleague who may certainly ask these questions, I wonder whether one should continue this way. We've already had a decision in the Mitar Vasiljevic trial, and as for the framework of the indictment for which this lady is now giving testimony, I wonder whether these questions about Mitar Vasiljevic are so important. I know she mentioned him, but I don't know if the Chamber can be helped with this. We have now to deal with Milan Lukic, with the two Lukics. There already has been a judgement for Vasiljevic, so is this helpful? Should one pursue along this line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ossogo, it goes to credibility, that's what he's -- that's why he's cross-examining. But I do believe you have spent enough time on that and should move on. He's testing her credibility; that's why he's referring to the Vasiljevic case, and he's entitled to do that but not ad nauseam.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Tell me when I'm beating the dead horse too much, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe you have done enough on that particular topic and should move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now today, Ms. 115, you indicate that you hid in an orchard --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sometimes it's a problem to have translation, full translation in B/C/S, so I kindly ask my learned friend to sometimes ask a little bit slowly to have a full translation in B/C/S. Thank you. Because it was overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, before we move on from the Bikavac fire would it be fair to say that these three paragraphs were all that you had read, reviewed, and otherwise attested to prior to this testimony today regarding the Bikavac fire? Ma'am, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is waiting for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that there's no mention of the garage door in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the garage door was mentioned in my full-length statement. When I was testifying in the Vasiljevic trial, I didn't have the opportunity to say anything about the Bikavac massacre. Judging by the extent you're asking questions about Mitar Vasiljevic, you are about to convict him yourself because you are insisting that I say that he was present. And I am mentioning the garage door because Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic dragged them there and put them against the door, the entrance door, of the house so that people couldn't escape. I could see that clearly. My vision was impaired in no way, and that is the part of my full-length statement as I made it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in your prior statement, ma'am, you mentioned no contact with VG-114, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you mention no grenades or gasoline bottles being thrown and seeing that, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did mention it today and that's what I said in my full-length statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: In your written statement in anticipation of your earlier testimony, isn't it true you did not mention grenades being used or gasoline bottles being used prior to today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm testifying today. This is the first opportunity I've had to testify about Bikavac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you had a full opportunity in over three days in the year 2000 to give all the details to the investigators that are relevant to this -- every incident that you knew of and you failed to do so; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did lots to that effect, I wrote entire novels. All these statements are, in fact, digested and I repeat that I'm saying the truth. I could write volumes and I have already forgotten lots of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, you had an opportunity to refresh your recollection with both the statement and your volumes of information, and you had an opportunity to give that information to the Prosecution in your proofing statement; and yet you only made one change in regards to the Bikavac in anticipation of today's testimony. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made no change. The Trial Chamber allowed me to speak at more length in my statement of today. I only spoke more extensively today and in comparison to my shorter statement, my earlier, shorter statement. I'm only sorry that I forgot many facts because a lot of time has elapsed since.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, if you read your statement as regards to the Bikavac fire, it appears in writing that you, in fact, saw nothing and left and only heard noises; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't leave the place in two minutes; that would have been impossible to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You made no mention of an orchard; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the shortest way. I didn't mention it, but it was a shortcut I took which I marked with a cross and a circle. That's where I -- the way I took to leave. It's a narrow footpath. I couldn't leave passing by the vehicles. It was a very small plum orchard on the plot belonging to Medo Mulahasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: In your statement you indicated that you heard bursts of fire but in today's testimony you indicated you saw the grenades and the fire and the gasoline bottles; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were throwing bottles filled with gasoline and hand-grenades and there were bursts of fire, and I was trying to make it to the main road which wasn't far from the orchard. It's all close, some 20 metres or so. I was going for the main road to continue toward the town centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true in your statement you did not indicate in any way that you saw this grenade throwing or gasoline throwing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reiterate that my statement was digested. Do I not have the right to say the truth today? Because I have been asked to give as much detail about the events at Bikavac. Why are you now questioning me thus and preventing me from saying the truth? I didn't do it, you didn't do it; we all know who did it, the two Lukics and the members of their group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You named several participants of or alleged participants of the Bikavac fire, including a Zoran Vasiljevic. Why did you hate Mr. Zoran Vasiljevic so much as you indicated in your prior direct testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for this question. Now I can say. To me that man is Zoran Vasiljevic. His name is Zoran, but I'm still not sure whether his last name is Simsic or Vasiljevic but I know what he looks like and I have a reason to hate that man (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) Similarly, as in the case of Mitar Vasiljevic or Knezevic. And please don't insult me because of these lowly people, not to call them animals. That is why I hate Zoran Vasiljevic or Knezevic. He is -- he lives somewhere around Belgrade. He is also a native of Visegrad who worked in Serbia and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, thank you. I believe you have given a full explanation to the question asked. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, ma'am, in your statement on page 17, you do indicate a synopsis about Mr. Vasiljevic, but you indicate that Mitar Vasiljevic was with him so it should be very easy for you to be able to tell them apart; wouldn't that be fair?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And if the court usher would change to page 17 if the witness needs to refresh her recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so you seem pretty certain as to the identities of both people (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were Mitar Knezevic, the older one, and Zoran Vasiljevic or Simsic. I'm sorry for not knowing his precise last name. It was Mitar Knezevic, the older man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You indicated in your earlier testimony the presence of Niko Vujicic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vujicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sorry, ma'am. And Veljko Planincic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Planincic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: They were both police officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the police in Visegrad at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander, the komandir, of the police was Milan Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What about Perisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Risto Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And Drago Tomic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He also had some senior post in the police. Yes, he too was with the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what about the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I don't know whether we dealt with all this, all these political questions regarding the structure of the police force. This lady was never asked any questions about the structure of the police forces in Visegrad. She did -- was asked questions about the persons that belonged to the police, but I believe that my fellow -- my learned colleague now is talking about the structure of the police force and this lady has nothing to do with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us see whether she can answer, whether she's able to answer the question. But we -- it's now time for the break, so we'll take the break, half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, you were about to ask the witness questions relating to the structure of the police force. To what end?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Basically, Your Honour, to show who was in control and that -- also this witness's knowledge of the situation in town at the time. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The trial is a public trial and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did I take us to the private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We need to be sure when the private session is ended that we return. It is, of course, ultimately the Chamber's responsibility but I ask all officers here to be alert to that and to bring it to the attention of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, did I do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that you did, but just let us know if we have not picked up that we are still in private session when we should not be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Ms. 115, I had asked you before about your knowledge of the Crisis Staff in Visegrad, the political hierarchy, if you will. Can you describe that at the time, in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must ask me specifically what it is that you're interested in in order for me to describe it. Is it the police, the staff, what specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What was the police -- what were Perisic's and Tomic's responsibility with regards to the police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Risto Perisic and Tomic, yes. Mr. Risto Perisic was the chief of the police of the so-called MUP, M-U-P, in Visegrad, a very positive person in my opinion. He discharged his duties, he did so in the very building of the police, he was responsible for his police force members in terms that they were to provide assistance and actually prove themselves as police officers in their activities. As for Dragan Tomic, I didn't know him well. In my view, he too was a very good person, a positive person, and I know that his brother was killed, I'm not sure and I apologise, whether it was his younger or older brother, he was killed in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what about the Crisis Staff, Savovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had occasion to see Savovic frequently. He worked at the municipality and he also discharged his office well, unassociated with the paramilitary forces, which is to say I cannot venture an opinion as to what actually Savovic did but he was a very positive person and figure in the city of Visegrad. At that time and during his time and after his time I can say that he was a very conscientious and clean person, a very positive character in my mind. According to what I heard and as far as I can remember and as far as I could see, in the electric power authority building radio waves could be used. There I often saw Savovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, ma'am, would it be fair to say that the Crisis Staff and -- placed into power Perisic and Tomic following the SDS taking power?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Perisic and Tomic were employed with the police prior to the breakout of the war, prior to the war situation. They did have power also before that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But after --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Crisis Staff did not actually confer any particular function on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the Crisis Staff had the ability through the SDS to appoint members throughout the community, this included the police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS was a distinct party, a separate party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Separate party from who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable to tell you anything about the SDS. That is something new. I was doing my job, Perisic was discharging his task. Now, the SDS was a new creation in town. I cannot tell you anything about it. I don't even know who was in charge of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true the SDS took control of Visegrad following the persecutions of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by took control --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please, Witness. Yes, Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, my learned friend Mr. Alarid is trying to get the witness to affirm that Muslims were persecuted by the SDS. I don't know whether in the examination-in-chief this was raised. I don't think it was raised at all. It might have to do with the credibility of the witness, but there are Rules of Procedure. You cannot go in any direction when you ask questions. The questions in the cross-examination have to do with the questions that were put in the examination-in-chief. I fully understood what you said earlier, but this is a different kettle of fish, if I could say so. I don't know where in my client's -- in my client's statement or testimony there's anything about the structure of all this. He's talking about persecution but not in such detail, so I believe that my learned friend should remain in the framework of the questions that were put in the examination-in-chief and in the statement. That way I think we could move on; otherwise, at this pace we're going to spend two days on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not going to allow -- I will not allow further questioning on that subject matter, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just to make the record and -- but I will move on is simply that in the global sense of a trial oftentimes the credibility is tested against other witnesses presented by the state. And when other witnesses have testified to different observations with regards to the make-up, the political structure, and then this witness is then somehow contradictory, then it would be up to the Chamber to weigh the credibility of each witness against the other and disregard one or the other or both, if necessary, if that's where -- if the Court saw fit down the road. That's where I was going with that, Your Honour, but I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, just in terms of your knowledge of Perisic, ma'am, did you realize he was a professor before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that he was a teacher, that he worked in a school, but I'm that kind of person and I didn't actually communicate much with Perisic, I didn't have the need to. I know that he was the chief of the police and that he conscientiously discharged his duties during the war, prior to the war, and after the war, according to what I know, because I had much more pressing matters to attend to, building my house, my duties at work. I was not involved in any political party so that I can only tell you what happened in the town of Visegrad when the people were divided. This is what I can tell you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, I'm going to ask you to try your best to give answers that are short and to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, do you recall testifying at the earlier trial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you recall being shown photographs in that trial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What photographs do you mean? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You were asked to look at a photograph and see if you could identify the location of the Pionirska Street fire.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that on that date you'd said that you could not identify where the fire had occurred because you had been too full of fear at the time that you witnessed it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was definitely scared, but I do know from which direction the fire came and whose property the house was and that's why I can find my way in that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The question was, ma'am, is: Isn't it true in the earlier trial you were not able to find that house in a photograph, and yet today you're able to point it out? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that I was unable to point to the house. Perhaps I wasn't, perhaps the photographs were not the same. Were they?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm simply confirming, ma'am, and it is not for me to say, it's actually for your recollection as a witness to know. And so isn't it true, ma'am, that you were not able to identify the home in the earlier trial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to stress again that I do not know. Perhaps I was unable to precisely point to the house. Perhaps the newly built house was pointed out to me, I -- in that photograph. Perhaps it was not this photograph which I just saw. Maybe I was shown one with a newly built house and I was unable to pin-point the two houses. I don't remember it well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, the matter could be clarified if you were to point us to the evidence in the earlier trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The evidence as it's loaded in my batch from the Prosecution, Your Honour, was -- it's under -- it's been uploaded under 1D00-0706, and if that could be brought on the screen by the court officer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you recall this photograph, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now that I'm looking at this photograph, whether it was the same photograph as on that day I don't remember; but I can recognise the house. The photograph may have been different. Now looking at it I can recognise the house. I don't remember my situation in the previous testimony, whether I was afraid or not, but now I can -- I can find my way in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What helped you gain this memory between the trial in 2001 and today, in 2008?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's because I am focused and I can think back more thoroughly so that -- so as to avoid pointing out the wrong house. Perhaps I meant a newly built house. There may be new houses there now. Looking at the houses as they are now, I cannot remember what the photograph was like that I saw several years ago. I don't remember well what exactly I said. I remember the main facts but not every word and everything that was written down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to disturb the cross-examination of my learned friend, but I didn't think he was going to show this document. I thought he was going to show the transcript. But since we have the document here on the screen, you see -- we see that the witness put a sign on the second house. Is this private session, sorry, are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
